1	-- Schema definitions and validators for SoraMech map files.
2	-- Validates box files, meta.json, and drivers.json against the spec
3	-- in docs/001-architecture.md. Used by both the runner and the server
4	-- before any file is written to disk.
5	
6	local DIR = "/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech"
7	
8	local M = {}
9	
10	-- {{{ valid_kinds
11	local valid_kinds = { call = true, data = true }
12	-- }}}
13	
14	-- {{{ valid_branches
15	-- null/nil means no comparator (single wire); the three strings are comparator outputs.
16	local valid_branches = { lt = true, eq = true, gt = true }
17	-- }}}
18	
19	-- {{{ err
20	local function err(errors, msg)
21	    errors[#errors + 1] = msg
22	end
23	-- }}}
24	
25	-- {{{ validate_connection
26	local function validate_connection(c, i, errors)
27	    -- from_branch is nil (no comparator) or one of "lt"/"eq"/"gt"
28	    if c.from_box == nil then
29	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'from_box'")
30	    end
31	    if c.from_branch ~= nil and not valid_branches[c.from_branch] then
32	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] 'from_branch' must be nil, 'lt', 'eq', or 'gt'")
33	    end
34	    if c.to_box == nil then
35	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'to_box'")
36	    end
37	    if c.to_input == nil then
38	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'to_input'")
39	    end
40	end
41	-- }}}
42	
43	-- {{{ validate_box
44	function M.validate_box(box)
45	    local errors = {}
46	    if type(box) ~= "table" then
47	        return { "box must be a table" }
48	    end
49	
50	    if box.id == nil or type(box.id) ~= "string" then
51	        err(errors, "missing or non-string 'id'")
52	    end
53	    if box.label == nil or type(box.label) ~= "string" then
54	        err(errors, "missing or non-string 'label'")
55	    end
56	    if box.kind == nil or not valid_kinds[box.kind] then
57	        err(errors, "missing or invalid 'kind' (must be 'call' or 'data')")
58	    end
59	
60	    if box.kind == "call" or box.kind == "data" then
61	        -- iterator boxes (issue 221) are a pure routing primitive: input
62	        -- copies straight to a chosen output, no language function is
63	        -- invoked. Such a box has no ref/fn — only `iterator_outputs`,
64	        -- an ordered list of output slot names. Otherwise ref is required.
65	        local is_iterator = box.iterator_outputs ~= nil
66	        if not is_iterator then
67	            if box.ref == nil or type(box.ref) ~= "string" then
68	                err(errors, "box missing 'ref'")
69	            end
70	        end
71	        if box.iterator_outputs ~= nil then
72	            if type(box.iterator_outputs) ~= "table" then
73	                err(errors, "'iterator_outputs' must be an array")
74	            else
75	                for i, name in ipairs(box.iterator_outputs) do
76	                    if type(name) ~= "string" then
77	                        err(errors, "'iterator_outputs[" .. i .. "]' must be a string")
78	                    end
79	                end
80	            end
81	        end
82	        -- fn is optional for binary callers (shell scripts, binaries)
83	        if box.inputs ~= nil and type(box.inputs) ~= "table" then
84	            err(errors, "'inputs' must be an array")
85	        end
86	        -- variadic_inputs: optional list of base names; each name must
87	        -- correspond to a series of inputs named "<base>_<index>" in
88	        -- box.inputs (the editor maintains this; we only check the
89	        -- shape here). See issue 217 part B.
90	        if box.variadic_inputs ~= nil then
91	            if type(box.variadic_inputs) ~= "table" then
92	                err(errors, "'variadic_inputs' must be an array")
93	            else
94	                for i, name in ipairs(box.variadic_inputs) do
95	                    if type(name) ~= "string" then
96	                        err(errors, "'variadic_inputs[" .. i .. "]' must be a string")
97	                    end
98	                end
99	            end
100	        end
101	        -- comparand: optional; if present it must be a string parseable as number at runtime
102	        if box.comparand ~= nil and type(box.comparand) ~= "string" then
103	            err(errors, "'comparand' must be a string")
104	        end
105	        -- has_output: optional; absence means "true" (default behavior).
106	        -- false marks a sink box whose function has no return values
107	        -- (issue 226); the runtime treats such boxes as terminal and the
108	        -- editor hides the output port and inspector output section.
109	        if box.has_output ~= nil and type(box.has_output) ~= "boolean" then
110	            err(errors, "'has_output' must be a boolean")
111	        end
112	        if box.connections ~= nil then
113	            for i, c in ipairs(box.connections) do
114	                validate_connection(c, i, errors)
115	            end
116	        end
117	    end
118	
119	    if box.ui ~= nil then
120	        if type(box.ui) ~= "table" then
121	            err(errors, "'ui' must be a table")
122	        elseif box.ui.x == nil or box.ui.y == nil then
123	            err(errors, "'ui' must have 'x' and 'y' fields")
124	        end
125	    end
126	
127	    return errors
128	end
129	-- }}}
130	
131	-- {{{ validate_meta
132	function M.validate_meta(meta)
133	    local errors = {}
134	    if type(meta) ~= "table" then
135	        return { "meta.json must be a table" }
136	    end
137	    if meta.name == nil or type(meta.name) ~= "string" then
138	        err(errors, "meta.json missing 'name'")
139	    end
140	    if meta.entry_box_id == nil or type(meta.entry_box_id) ~= "string" then
141	        err(errors, "meta.json missing 'entry_box_id'")
142	    end
143	    return errors
144	end
145	-- }}}
146	
147	-- {{{ validate_drivers
148	function M.validate_drivers(drivers)
149	    local errors = {}
150	    if type(drivers) ~= "table" then
151	        return { "drivers.json must be a table" }
152	    end
153	    for ext, path in pairs(drivers) do
154	        if type(ext) ~= "string" or ext:sub(1, 1) ~= "." then
155	            err(errors, "driver key '" .. tostring(ext) .. "' must be a dot-prefixed extension")
156	        end
157	        if type(path) ~= "string" then
158	            err(errors, "driver value for '" .. ext .. "' must be a string path")
159	        end
160	    end
161	    return errors
162	end
163	-- }}}
164	
165	return M

None of the three knows about the others\nat runtime.\n\n```\n  Browser (assets/index.html)\n       |  HTTP (file CRUD)\n       v\n  src/006-server-main.lua       [map directory]\n                                maps/<name>/\n                                  meta.json\n                                  boxes/\n                                  data/\n                                  src/\n                                  compiled/   (after compile button)\n                                  tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/\n       ^\n       | reads & writes\n  Runner (one of):\n    src/007-runner-main.lua     ← phase 2, synchronous Lua interpreter\n    soramech-pool (binary)      ← phase 3, C thread pool runner\n```\n\n### src/006-server-main.lua (the editor's HTTP backend)\n\nThin file CRUD proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and\ntranslates them into reads and writes on the map directory. No logic\nbeyond path validation and basic consistency checks (e.g. reject a\ndelete if the box is still referenced by another box's connection\nlist).\n\nStarted with: `luajit src/006-server-main.lua [port]` (default 7700).\nThe `run` script at the project root starts the server and opens the\neditor.\n\nThe editor is editor-only — no run button, no run results display.\nThe runner is invoked separately, by command line. `last-run.jsonl`\nis the runner's output, consumed by external tooling, not by the\neditor.\n\n### Phase 2 runner — `src/007-runner-main.lua`\n\nSynchronous Lua interpreter. Loads a map directory, validates the\ngraph, walks boxes in dependency order, invokes language drivers per\nbox (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/c.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`). Each box\ninvocation is wrapped in a `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary that\nmatches the phase 3 thread pool's action signature.\n\nThis is the development target while the editor is being built out.\nPhase 2 retires wholesale when phase 3 lands; the editor and the\nmap-directory format are unchanged across the cutover.\n\n### Phase 3 runner — `soramech-pool` (`src/008-pool-runner.c`)\n\nThe phase 3 runner is a single C binary. It owns:\n\n- A **SoraMech-built thread pool** under `libs/task-pool/` (3d-rts at\n  `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n  is the design reference, not vendored).\n- A **C graph loader** (`src/graph-loader.c`) — replaces\n  `src/003-loader.lua`. The runner has no embedded Lua state at the\n  top level; Lua only appears inside a Lua language spec's per-worker\n  handle.\n- A **per-input-port slot store** (`src/slot-store.c`) — ring-buffer\n  cells in process heap, durable for the run, plus a large-value heap\n  for variable-size payloads.\n- A **dispatch layer** (`src/dispatch.c`) — the single worker-side\n  action: read inputs → invoke spec → pick branch → push outputs.\n- A **language spec registry** (`src/spec-registry.c`) — `dlopen`s\n  every `langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup and registers it by name\n  and file extension.\n- A **run-output writer** — a dedicated thread that drains a\n  multi-producer-single-consumer ring of events and appends one JSON\n  line per event to `tmp/last-run.jsonl`.\n\nOne pool per map run. Created after the graph loads and validates;\ndestroyed after the active-task counter reaches zero. Worker count\ndefaults to logical CPUs (capped at `MAX_WORKERS=16`), overridable\nvia `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\nSee \"Execution model — phase 3\" below for the action loop and slot\nmechanics.\n\n### assets/index.html (the editor)\n\nStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\nTalks to `src/006-server-main.lua` for all file operations. No run\nbutton. The Compile button (added in phase 2 as UI only) wires into\nthe phase 3 build/package pipeline once it lands.\n\n## Map directory format\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n  meta.json          — { name, description, src_dirs?, lang? }\n  boxes/\n    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n  data/\n    <name>.json      — soramech-data tables; section-level \"constant\" flag\n  src/\n    *.lua, *.c, *.sh — box function source files\n  compiled/          — produced by the compile pipeline (issue 309)\n    pool-runner      — copy or symlink of soramech-pool\n    src/             — every source file the map uses\n    bin/             — compiled .so files (C boxes via the C spec's compile callback)\n    langs/<name>/    — copy of each language spec .so the map uses\n    manifest.json    — every box, its language, its artifact path, build version\n  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n    last-run.jsonl   — phase 3 run log (JSON Lines)\n    logs/            — additional run logs\n```\n\nA compiled map runs standalone: `./compiled/pool-runner` looks up its\nspecs in `compiled/langs/`, reads `manifest.json`, and executes\nwithout any reference to the live editor source tree.\n\nPhase 2's `drivers.json` file is gone. Phase 2 resolves drivers by\nfile extension via the `drivers/` directory; phase 3 resolves\nlanguages by file extension via the spec registry (each spec declares\nits `file_ext`). No map-local driver config file is needed in either\nphase.\n\nThe `data/` directory is for `soramech-data` storage (see \"Data\nfiles\" below). It is **not** where file-source boxes read from — those\nread arbitrary paths, see Box kinds.\n\n## Box file format\n\nEvery box is a single JSON file under `boxes/<id>.json`. Every box\nhas exactly **one output wire** (issue 218). There is no `outputs`\narray. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output\nwire as one value; multi-value returns are encoded as JSON (or a\nlanguage-native struct on a same-language wire — see \"Language spec\nsystem\" below) and decoded downstream.\n\n### Box kinds\n\n| `kind`       | Runs a function? | Notes                                                          |\n|--------------|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `call`       | yes              | Plain call, comparator, iterator, etc. — see `routing` below.  |\n| `data`       | no               | Language-agnostic **file source**. Reads `path` at dispatch.   |\n| `file_write` | no               | Language-agnostic **file sink**. Writes inputs to disk.        |\n\n`data` and `file_write` are dispatch-layer primitives — the runtime\nreads/writes the file directly, no language spec is invoked. Both\nfollow atomic-write semantics where it matters (write to `path.tmp`,\nfsync, rename).\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"config\", \"kind\": \"data\", \"path\": \"config.json\",\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"save\",   \"kind\": \"file_write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"path\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n    { \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 400, \"y\": 100 } }\n```\n\n`data` has `path` (not `ref`), no `fn`, no inputs; emits the file's\nbytes-as-UTF-8 string on its one output wire. `file_write` takes\n`path` and `text` as inputs; the `path` input can be wired (dynamic)\nor filled by a literal (static). Binary files are out of scope for\nboth — non-UTF-8 reads fail with a clear error.\n\n### Call boxes and the `routing` field\n\nA `call` box runs a function (`ref` + `fn`) and produces one output\nvalue. The `routing` field decides where that value goes. Every\ncall box carries `routing` explicitly — there is no implicit default:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"plain-call\", \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\", \"fn\": \"trim\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"plain-call\", \"from_branch\": null,\n      \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"text\" }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 } }\n```\n\nThe function **always runs**, regardless of routing kind. Routing\ndecides which downstream branch receives the function's output; the\nfunction itself doesn't know.\n\n#### Routing kinds\n\n| `routing.kind`  | Output ports          | Branch picker                                                | Status     |\n|-----------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|------------|\n| `plain`         | single port           | fan to all outgoing wires                                    | shipped    |\n| `comparator`    | `lt` / `eq` / `gt`    | `compare(output, comparand)` → lt/eq/gt                      | shipped    |\n| `iterator`      | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, N)`                             | shipped    |\n| `randomizer`    | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | `hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % N`                 | follow-on  |\n| `weighted`      | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to PRECISION | follow-on  |\n| `distributor`   | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | argmin over downstream slot fill levels                      | follow-on  |\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": \"0\" }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\",   \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"weighted\",   \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2] }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n**Branch-level fan-out**: for `comparator` / `iterator` / etc., each\nbranch port acts like a small plain output of its own. If the\ncomparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three consumers, then\non every invocation where the routing decision picks `lt`, all three\nof those wires fire. The routing decision picks which branch;\nfan-out picks which consumers on that branch receive the value.\n\nPlain output port can fan freely too — multiple connections from\n`from_branch: null` send copies to every wired consumer. Pulling\nmultiple wires from a single output is not a routing decision.\n\n### Input ports\n\n```json\n\"inputs\": [\n  { \"name\": \"text\",        \"type\": \"string\" },\n  { \"name\": \"config_path\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true,\n    \"value\": \"config.json\" }\n]\n```\n\nEvery input port is in one of three states at compile time:\n\n1. A wire is connected to it.\n2. A literal `value` is set on it.\n3. It carries `optional: true`.\n\n**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The\nerror is precise: which box, which port. Enforced at the Compile\nbutton (phase 2 UI / phase 3 build) and again in the C graph loader\nat runtime — belt and suspenders against hand-edited maps.\n\n`optional: true` does **not** mean \"pass null\" — it means the\nargument doesn't have to be passed. The dispatch layer assembles\n`input_data[]` / `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually have\nvalues; an absent optional port shortens `n_inputs` by one and the\nlanguage's native short-arg convention handles the rest. Each\nlanguage picks up the convention natively (Lua: missing args are\n`nil`; Bash: positional unset; C: wrapper reads `n_inputs` and\nforwards what's present).\n\nNull as an **explicit** value (typed `null` into the literal field)\nis a different thing: it arrives through the function call as a real\nargument, mapped to the language's native null (Lua `nil`, Bash empty\nstring `\"\"`, C `NULL`).\n\nVariadic inputs (`variadic_inputs`) carry base names whose ports\nexpand to `<base>_0`, `<base>_1`, … in the editor (issue 217).\n\n### Connections\n\nConnections are written to **both** endpoint box files. The loader\nvalidates at load time that both ends agree — disagreement is a\nhard error.\n\n```json\n{ \"from_box\": \"...\",\n  \"from_branch\": null | \"lt\" | \"eq\" | \"gt\" | \"out_0\" | ...,\n  \"to_box\":   \"...\",\n  \"to_input\": \"...\" }\n```\n\n`from_branch` is `null` for `routing: plain` and for boxes without a\nrouting field; otherwise it names the branch port the wire leaves\nfrom.\n\n## Language spec system (phase 3)\n\nEach language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol. The pool\nrunner loads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen` and\nregisters it by `name` (for box lookup) and `file_ext` (for source\nresolution). The spec contract is uniform across languages; no\nlanguage is privileged. The runner itself does not link to liblua,\nlibc++, or any language-specific runtime — only specs do.\n\n### `lang_spec_t`\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Pool startup calls init() for every spec on\n    // every worker before unblocking the init barrier; teardown()\n    // runs at shutdown.\n    void *(*init)    (int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: at map-compile time. C uses this to gcc -shared -fPIC.\n    // Lua and Bash leave this NULL.\n    int   (*compile) (const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // Universal invoke path: JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out.\n    // Used across every cross-language wire.\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle,\n                           const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                           const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                           void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n\n    // Fast invoke path: language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out.\n    // Used when producer and consumer share a language (see \"Same-language\n    // wire fast path\" below).\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* same signature */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary.\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke_*` is a fatal error. The dispatch\nlayer prints the context (box id, function name, language) and\naborts. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task \"failed\" state.\nBugs do not belong in production.\n\n### Init barrier\n\nWorkers are not safe to dispatch to until every worker has completed\n`init` for every spec the map uses. Pool startup runs each worker's\n`init` calls, increments a shared `workers_ready` atomic, and blocks\non a condition variable. The main thread waits for\n`workers_ready == n_workers`, then broadcasts — all workers release\ntogether and begin pulling tasks. One-shot; doesn't re-engage.\n\n### Same-language wire fast path\n\nWire format defaults to JSON. At compile time, every wire is\nclassified `fast_path: true` (same language at both ends) or `false`\n(crosses a language boundary). The compile step also records the\nproducer's `output_format` per box — `native` if **all** consumers\nof its output share its language, `json` if any consumer is\ndifferent.\n\nAt runtime:\n\n- `fast_path && output_format=native`: producer writes native bytes;\n  same-language consumers read native bytes directly.\n- `output_format=json`: producer writes JSON bytes; cross-language\n  consumers read directly; same-language consumers call\n  `json_to_native` on the way in.\n\nPer-language native forms:\n- **Lua** — `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables,\n  raw bytes for strings/numbers.\n- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct (the C spec's `compile`\n  callback knows the types).\n- **Bash** — strings only; the fast path is an alias of the JSON\n  path.\n\nA spec that only ever talks to itself can stub out `invoke_json`\n(compile error if a cross-language wire ever points at it). A spec\nthat participates in cross-language wires must implement all four\ncallbacks.\n\n### Shipped specs\n\n`langs/lua/spec.so`, `langs/c/spec.so`, `langs/bash/spec.so` ship as\nreference implementations:\n\n- **Lua** — `init` constructs a `lua_State`; `invoke_*` does\n  `luaL_loadfile` (cached) + `lua_pcall`.\n- **C** — `compile` runs `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out> <src>` (caching\n  by mtime); `invoke_*` does `dlsym` + direct call through a wrapper\n  the compile step generates from the box signature.\n- **Bash** — `init` spawns a persistent bash subprocess and connects\n  to it over a Unix domain socket. `invoke_*` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response. The same shape every future\n  non-embeddable-runtime language uses (Python optional, Node\n  optional, etc.).\n\nA user adds a new language by writing a `langs/<name>/spec.c` and a\nsmall Makefile. SoraMech itself does not transpile box source between\nlanguages.\n\n## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)\n\nThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the boxes that have all\ntheir inputs satisfied. Each box call:\n\n1. Read wired output values from predecessor boxes.\n2. Shell out to the appropriate driver script (`drivers/<lang>.sh`).\n3. Decode the single JSON value from driver stdout.\n4. Hold the output in runner memory, keyed by box id.\n5. Fire connections — enqueue boxes whose inputs are now met.\n\nSingle-threaded; one process per box call. The `task_fn` boundary\nmatches the phase 3 dispatch action signature, so the executor can\nbe swapped without changing the box execution model.\n\n## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n\nTasks are ephemeral; box state is durable. Each box owns one slot\nper input port plus optional state (iterator counter, language\nhandle). A **task** is one stack frame on a worker — `box_id` is\nall it carries. Tasks come and go; boxes persist for the run.\n\n### Slots\n\nEvery input port has exactly one slot, allocated at graph load and\nfreed at run end. A wire is a routing declaration; the producer\ndoesn't own a slot — its output is a push event into every\ndownstream input slot it's wired to. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is\nN producers pushing into one slot.\n\nSlot modes:\n\n| Mode                    | Cells   | Reads via         | Used for                                    |\n|-------------------------|---------|-------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n| 1-cell peek             | 1       | `slot_peek`       | Literals; wires from runs-once producers    |\n| N-cell pop              | N       | `slot_pop`        | Wires whose producer runs many times        |\n| `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`   | 1 atom  | `slot_read_inc`   | Iterator / randomizer / weighted counters   |\n\nCompile-time analysis decides per wire: a producer is \"runs-once\" if\nno transitive ancestor is an iterator, else \"runs-N-times.\" The\nformer gets a 1-cell peek slot (subsequent consumer tasks re-read the\nsame value); the latter gets an N-cell ring (FIFO drain, one cell\nper consumer task).\n\nVariable-size payloads (long LLM outputs, dynamically-sized arrays)\nlive in a separate **large-value heap**. The slot then holds a small\nfixed-size handle `{ uint32_t size; uint32_t offset; }`. The slot\nallocator only ever sees fixed-size slots; the two-tier scheme keeps\nthe hot path simple while supporting unbounded values.\n\n### Cell tagging for parallel iterators\n\nEach cell optionally carries a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\ndata. Iterator pushes carry their counter value as the tag; slots\ndownstream of an iterator are allocated with `SLOT_TAGGED`, and\n`slot_pop` on a tagged slot returns the **lowest-tag** cell — not\nthe head. This preserves iteration order across parallel iterator\nworkers (task K of iterator A may push before task K-1 if it landed\non a faster worker; the tag makes the consumer see the values in\niteration order regardless).\n\nWhen a consumer has two tagged inputs from two iterators, each port\npops in tag order independently — pairing falls out as `(A_K, B_K)`\nfor every K.\n\n### The dispatch action\n\nOne C function, one phase per worker per task:\n\n1. **Read inputs.** For each input port: `slot_peek` (peek mode) or\n   `slot_pop` (pop mode) into a heap buffer. Tasks are spawned only\n   when every input slot has a value (spawn-on-input-ready rule), so\n   no waiting is needed.\n2. **Invoke spec.** Look up the box's `lang`, find the worker's\n   handle for it, call `invoke_native` or `invoke_json` (per the\n   wire's fast-path classification). Output lands in a heap buffer\n   sized to the box's declared output size, or into the large-value\n   heap if the box's output is variable-size.\n3. **Pick the branch.** Dispatch on `routing.kind`:\n   - `plain`: every outgoing wire fires.\n   - `comparator`: compare to `comparand`, fire only `lt`/`eq`/`gt`.\n   - `iterator`: `idx = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs)`,\n     fire `out_idx` only.\n   - `randomizer` / `weighted` / `distributor`: kind-specific rule\n     (computes an `idx` from the counter slot or from downstream\n     fill, fires that branch).\n4. **Push.** For each firing wire, `slot_push` into the consumer's\n   input slot. The push carries the appropriate ordering tag\n   (iterator counter snapshot for iterator-rooted wires; 0 for\n   plain). Each push triggers a spawn-on-input-ready check on the\n   consumer; if the check passes, the dispatch layer spawns a new\n   `dispatch_task_t` and the pool picks it up.\n5. **Done.** The action returns; the pool decrements the active-task\n   counter. The action does not block, does not wait, does not park.\n\n### Startup, quiescence, and termination\n\nStartup: the pool runner pushes literal-input values into the\ncorresponding slots, then spawns first tasks for boxes whose input\nsets are now satisfied. Iterator counter slots start at 0.\n\nQuiescence: the main thread waits on a condition variable that\nsignals when the pool's active-task counter reaches zero with no\npending spawns. That's the run-over signal. The graph validator at\nload time rejects non-iterator cycles, so the run cannot deadlock —\nan iterator with no upstream pushes simply contributes nothing\nfurther, and once the counter drains, termination fires.\n\nHard-crash error policy: a nonzero `invoke_*` return aborts the\nprocess. No retry, no per-task failed state, no fallback executor.\n\n### Blocking-aware iterator pattern\n\nLong-running operations (network calls, LLM inference) hold their\nworker for the duration. Pool size is the budget. The cooperative\npattern for not holding a worker for minutes: split the call into a\n\"kickoff\" box and a \"check-done\" iterator that polls. Each pass\nthrough the iterator releases the worker between checks. Documented\nfully in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n## Run output — `tmp/last-run.jsonl`\n\nPhase 3 writes one JSON object per event, one event per line, to\n`tmp/last-run.jsonl`. The format decouples the runner from the\neditor — the editor never displays run results; the file is for LLM\nconsumption, CLI viewers, and the integration test harness.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":..., \"map\":\"maps/<name>\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\"}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",  \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",    \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",  \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}   // SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\",   \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}                              // SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1\n{\"event\":\"run_end\",     \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nMechanism: a dedicated writer thread drains a multi-producer\nsingle-consumer ring buffer of fixed-size event records, serializes\neach to JSON, and appends to the file. Workers push records into the\nring without contending on a file mutex. The writer joins before\n`pool_destroy`, including a final `run_end` summary.\n\nInputs/outputs per task are off by default (`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`\nto enable; truncated past 4 KB). Slot allocator events are off by\ndefault (`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` to enable). Timestamps are Unix\nepoch floats.\n\nThe file is overwritten on every run. Rotation is out of scope —\nusers who want history copy the file.\n\n## Build & compile pipeline\n\nA top-level `Makefile` builds:\n\n1. `soramech-pool` — statically links the pool, JSON parser, slot\n   store, graph loader, dispatch layer, spec registry.\n2. `langs/<name>/spec.so` — per-spec, via the per-language Makefile\n   (Lua links LuaJIT; C links `-ldl`; Bash links nothing extra).\n\nModes: `make` (release, `-O2 -Wall`), `make DEBUG=1` (`-O0 -g`),\n`make STRICT=1` (release + `-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n\nVendored dependencies (the task pool, the JSON parser) live under\n`libs/` as plain source — no submodules, no fetches at build time.\n\nSpec discovery at runtime: the runner reads `/proc/self/exe`,\nfollows the symlink, and scans for `langs/` next to its own binary.\n`SORAMECH_LANGS_DIR=/path/to/langs` overrides for development.\n\n### Compile a map for standalone execution\n\n`./compiled/pool-runner` runs a map independently of the editor and\nthe surrounding source tree. The compile step (Compile button in the\neditor, or `soramech-compile <map-dir>` from the CLI) produces:\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/compiled/\n  pool-runner          ← copy or symlink of soramech-pool\n  src/                 ← every source file the map uses\n  bin/                 ← per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n  langs/<name>/spec.so ← one per language the map uses\n  manifest.json        ← every box, its language, artifact path, build version\n```\n\nSteps: walk the graph (reusing the C loader's validation); copy\nsource files and transitive `require` / `#include` dependencies;\ninvoke each spec's `compile` callback for boxes whose language needs\nit; copy the spec `.so` files used by the map; copy or symlink the\nrunner binary; write the manifest. Per-box artifacts mtime-compare\nso a re-compile recompiles only what changed. Any failure aborts\nthe step and leaves the partial output for inspection but does not\nwrite the manifest, so the deployment is recognizably broken until\na clean compile succeeds.\n\n## Data files\n\nPersistent data lives in `data/<name>.json` and is accessed via\n`libs/soramech-data.lua` (`data.get` / `data.set` / `data.load`).\nFormat:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only;\nfield-level `constant` flags individual fields within an otherwise\nmutable file. This is **separate** from the `data` box kind (which\nreads arbitrary files at the dispatch layer) — `soramech-data` is\nthe per-map structured-table store; `data` boxes are unstructured\nfile sources.\n\nEphemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, `last-run.jsonl`) goes to\n`tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives the run but not a\nreboot — intentionally.\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/001-architecture.md"
}

Base directory for this skill: /home/ritz/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/frontend-design/1c81b812991b/skills/frontend-design

This skill guides creation of distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces that avoid generic "AI slop" aesthetics. Implement real working code with exceptional attention to aesthetic details and creative choices.

The user provides frontend requirements: a component, page, application, or interface to build. They may include context about the purpose, audience, or technical constraints.

## Design Thinking

Before coding, understand the context and commit to a BOLD aesthetic direction:
- **Purpose**: What problem does this interface solve? Who uses it?
- **Tone**: Pick an extreme: brutally minimal, maximalist chaos, retro-futuristic, organic/natural, luxury/refined, playful/toy-like, editorial/magazine, brutalist/raw, art deco/geometric, soft/pastel, industrial/utilitarian, etc. There are so many flavors to choose from. Use these for inspiration but design one that is true to the aesthetic direction.
- **Constraints**: Technical requirements (framework, performance, accessibility).
- **Differentiation**: What makes this UNFORGETTABLE? What's the one thing someone will remember?

**CRITICAL**: Choose a clear conceptual direction and execute it with precision. Bold maximalism and refined minimalism both work - the key is intentionality, not intensity.

Then implement working code (HTML/CSS/JS, React, Vue, etc.) that is:
- Production-grade and functional
- Visually striking and memorable
- Cohesive with a clear aesthetic point-of-view
- Meticulously refined in every detail

## Frontend Aesthetics Guidelines

Focus on:
- **Typography**: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices that elevate the frontend's aesthetics; unexpected, characterful font choices. Pair a distinctive display font with a refined body font.
- **Color & Theme**: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency. Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes.
- **Motion**: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only solutions for HTML. Use Motion library for React when available. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered micro-interactions. Use scroll-triggering and hover states that surprise.
- **Spatial Composition**: Unexpected layouts. Asymmetry. Overlap. Diagonal flow. Grid-breaking elements. Generous negative space OR controlled density.
- **Backgrounds & Visual Details**: Create atmosphere and depth rather than defaulting to solid colors. Add contextual effects and textures that match the overall aesthetic. Apply creative forms like gradient meshes, noise textures, geometric patterns, layered transparencies, dramatic shadows, decorative borders, custom cursors, and grain overlays.

NEVER use generic AI-generated aesthetics like overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts), cliched color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds), predictable layouts and component patterns, and cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character.

Interpret creatively and make unexpected choices that feel genuinely designed for the context. No design should be the same. Vary between light and dark themes, different fonts, different aesthetics. NEVER converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations.

**IMPORTANT**: Match implementation complexity to the aesthetic vision. Maximalist designs need elaborate code with extensive animations and effects. Minimalist or refined designs need restraint, precision, and careful attention to spacing, typography, and subtle details. Elegance comes from executing the vision well.

Remember: Claude is capable of extraordinary creative work. Don't hold back, show what can truly be created when thinking outside the box and committing fully to a distinctive vision.

12	- Run `luajit src/007-runner-main.lua <map-dir>` to execute the map
13	- Add a custom language driver and have the runner use it

16	
17	Demo: `issues/completed/demos/phase-1/`.
18	
19	## Phase 2 — Editor & graph model (current)
20	
21	Goal: an editor you can actually use to build maps, and the graph
22	model the phase 3 runtime will consume.
23	
24	This phase is editor-focused with some graph-model cleanup:
25	- Map picker, fit-to-view, interaction hints, entry-box marking
26	- Source file browser with auto-populated input ports
27	- File browser library directories
28	- Single-output driver contract (issue 218)
29	- Comparator-based branching replaces the old `branch` box kind with

33	- Variadic / queued inputs (issues 213, 217)
34	- Compile button (issue 222) — placeholder until phase 3's build
35	  system (issue 309) ships the backing endpoint
36	- Ollama / LLM library (issue 209)
37	
38	Phase 2 runs on the synchronous Lua interpreter
39	(`src/007-runner-main.lua`). No threading. Drivers per phase 1.

41	See `issues/phase-2-progress.md` for the live status.
42	
43	## Phase 3 — Thread pool runtime (planned, fully designed)
44	
45	Goal: replace the Lua synchronous runner with a C thread pool runner
46	that executes box graphs in parallel, with persistent per-worker
47	language runtimes and proper inter-task value plumbing.
48	
49	Designed across issues 301–311:
50	
51	- 301 — pool lifecycle and per-worker init
52	- 302 — wire value slot store (per-task ring buffers, refcount,
53	  large-value heap)
54	- 303 — language runtime spec (`lang_spec_t` interface)
55	- 304 — task dispatch layer
56	- 305 — C graph loader (replaces `src/003-loader.lua`)
57	- 306 — Lua language spec (in-process via `lua_State`)
58	- 307 — C language spec (in-process via `dlopen`, with compile)
59	- 308 — Bash language spec (out-of-process via Unix domain socket)
60	- 309 — build system & Makefile orchestration
61	- 310 — priority queue (wired in, no-op behaviorally)
62	- 311 — integration tests & run output (`last-run.jsonl`)
63	
64	When phase 3 lands, the synchronous Lua runner retires. The editor

79	- Streaming output from SoraMind inference back to the runner

1	# SoraMech — Language Driver System
2	
3	## Two systems, one filename
4	
5	Phase 2 used **driver scripts** — shell wrappers under `drivers/`
6	that the synchronous runner invoked one process per box call.
7	
8	Phase 3 uses **language specs** — `.so` libraries under `langs/`
9	loaded by the C pool runner via `dlopen`, with persistent per-worker
10	runtimes.
11	
12	Same idea, different mechanism. Phase 3 replaces phase 2 wholesale
13	when it lands. This document covers both, since the project lives in
14	phase 2 today and the phase 3 design is fully specified.
15	
16	## Phase 2 — Driver scripts (current)
17	
18	A driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one
19	language. The synchronous runner looks up the file extension, finds
20	the driver script, and calls it.
21	
22	### Driver contract
23	
24	The runner invokes a driver as:
25	
26	```
27	<driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg> ...]
28	```
29	
30	Arguments are always strings. Structured values (tables, arrays) are
31	passed as JSON strings and decoded by the driver.
32	
33	The driver must:
34	- Exit 0 on success, nonzero on failure
35	- Print one JSON value to stdout — string, number, boolean, object,
36	  or null. One output wire per box.
37	- Print error messages to stderr on failure
38	
39	Multi-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly
40	one output wire (issue 218).
41	
42	### Built-in driver scripts
43	
44	Shipped in the project's `drivers/` directory:
45	
46	- `drivers/lua.sh` — invokes a Lua function via `luajit`
47	- `drivers/c.sh` — compiles `.c` (mtime cache) and runs the binary
48	- `drivers/bash.sh` — sources the `.sh` and calls the function
49	
50	User-added drivers go in the same directory and are picked up by
51	extension.
52	
53	### What's wrong with this model
54	
55	Process spawn cost dominates each call (1–10 ms per language).
56	Stdout is a fragile channel — debug prints inside box code corrupt
57	the wire value. Each invocation is its own fresh interpreter; there
58	is no persistent runtime between calls. These are the limitations
59	phase 3 fixes.
60	
61	## Phase 3 — Language specs (planned)
62	
63	Each language is a small C library implementing the spec interface
64	defined in issue 303. The pool runner loads every
65	`langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup; the spec interface is uniform
66	across languages, with no privileged language.
67	
68	### Spec interface
69	
70	```c
71	typedef struct {
72	    const char *name;
73	    const char *file_ext;
74	
75	    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);
76	    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);
77	    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,
78	                     const box_t *box);
79	    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,
80	                    const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,
81	                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,
82	                    int n_inputs,
83	                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity,
84	                    int *out_size);
85	} lang_spec_t;
86	```
87	
88	`init` runs once per worker thread at pool startup. `teardown` runs
89	at shutdown. `compile` runs at map load time for languages that need
90	it (C). `invoke` runs once per box invocation.
91	
92	The spec receives input bytes and writes output bytes — never
93	interacts with slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads
94	inputs from slots into byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, takes
95	back bytes, writes them to the output slot.
96	
97	### Reference specs
98	
99	- **Lua** (issue 306) — handle is a `lua_State` per worker. `invoke`
100	  loads the box file (cached in the registry), pushes typed
101	  arguments, calls via `lua_pcall`, serializes the return value.
102	- **C** (issue 307) — handle is a `dlopen`-cache per worker.
103	  `compile` generates a wrapper from the box's declared inputs and
104	  return type, then runs `cc` to produce the `.so`. `invoke` does
105	  `dlsym` and a direct function-pointer call.
106	- **Bash** (issue 308) — handle is a Unix domain socket connected
107	  to a persistent `bash-server.sh` subprocess. `invoke` sends a
108	  framed request, reads a framed response.
109	
110	The Lua and C specs are in-process (Option 1 in
111	`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`). The Bash spec is out-of-process
112	(Option 3) — proof that the spec interface accommodates languages
113	that cannot be embedded.
114	
115	### Adding a new language
116	
117	A user adds Python, Rust, or anything else by writing a new spec:
118	
119	1. Create `langs/<name>/spec.c` implementing the four callbacks.
120	2. Create `langs/<name>/Makefile` that builds `spec.so`.
121	3. Add the language to `meta.json src_dirs` if necessary so the
122	   editor's file browser can see source files.
123	
124	The pool runner picks up the new spec at the next startup. No
125	SoraMech code change required.
126	
127	For full implementation guidance, see the future
128	`docs/005-language-specs.md` (referenced from issue 303). For the
129	spec contract itself, issue 303.
130	
131	## Migration: phase 2 → phase 3
132	
133	When phase 3 lands:
134	
135	| Phase 2                              | Phase 3                              |
136	|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
137	| `drivers/lua.sh`                     | `langs/lua/spec.so`                  |
138	| `drivers/c.sh`                       | `langs/c/spec.so`                    |
139	| `drivers/bash.sh`                    | `langs/bash/spec.so`                 |
140	| `drivers.json` (per-map)             | (none — spec registry is global)     |
141	| stdout as channel                    | direct function call / Unix socket   |
142	| One process per call                 | Persistent runtimes                  |
143	| Single output wire (JSON-encoded)    | Single output slot (typed bytes)     |
144	
145	Box JSON does not change shape — `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`
146	remain. Phase 3 reads the same files phase 2 reads. The runtime
147	mechanism beneath the box is what changes.
148	
149	## Relevant issues
150	
151	- 102 (completed) — phase 2 driver interface
152	- 218 (completed) — single-output driver contract
153	- 303 — phase 3 language spec contract
154	- 306 — Lua language spec
155	- 307 — C language spec
156	- 308 — Bash language spec
157	
```

1	# SoraMech — IPC and Threading Model
2	
3	## The problem
4	
5	The current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to
6	a driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The
7	return value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:
8	
9	1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending
10	   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,
11	   not by the actual work.
12	
13	2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output
14	   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is
15	   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.
16	
17	The goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,
18	and the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## The threading roadmap
23	
24	Three stages, each building on the last:
25	
26	**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the
27	graph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is
28	the task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.
29	
30	**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine
31	scheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.
32	LuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is
33	waiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural
34	concurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.
35	
36	**Stage 3 — SoraMech-owned thread pool.** A pool implementation
37	written for SoraMech, with the 3d-rts pool design as a reference.
38	The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread pool. Worker threads pull
39	tasks from the pool; OS-level scheduling replaces any single-threaded
40	ordering. Cross-language calls block a worker thread while other
41	threads continue. True parallelism across cores.
42	
43	Effil-jit is not used. Coroutines are not used. The path goes
44	straight from synchronous (phase 2) to the C pool (phase 3) — no
45	intermediate coroutine stage.
46	
47	---
48	
49	## Stage 3 detail: pthreads task model
50	
51	Each box execution in the thread pool is a **task struct** containing:
52	
53	- **Function pointer** — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C
54	  function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)
55	- **Shared memory pointer** — the region holding the input arguments and
56	  return value for this invocation
57	- **Dependency list** — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on
58	- **Waiting list** — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task
59	- **Counter** (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated
60	  in-place when the iterator re-queues itself
61	
62	Task structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per
63	invocation). They live for the entire run.
64	
65	### Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions
66	
67	When a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed
68	in its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no
69	allocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.
70	
71	When an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared
72	memory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task
73	queue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is
74	unchanged; only its position in the queue changes.
75	
76	This means "blocked", "queued", and "running" are states defined by which
77	list a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.
78	
79	### Per-thread language runtimes
80	
81	Each worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:
82	- **Lua:** one `lua_State` per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but
83	  one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box
84	  function via `lua_pcall`.
85	- **C:** the compiled box function is called directly through the function
86	  pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.
87	- **Bash/other:** a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket
88	  server model — see Option 3 above). The task wrapper sends a request and
89	  blocks the thread waiting for the response.
90	
91	### Iterator self-re-queue
92	
93	An iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it
94	completes:
95	1. It increments its `counter` field in-place (or wraps to 0).
96	2. It checks its input queue for the next pending value.
97	3. If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself
98	   to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters
99	   the queue with updated state.
100	4. If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting
101	   list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.
102	
103	Input values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued
104	inputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the
105	counter and firing a different output path each time.
106	
107	### Blocking semantics for long-running operations
108	
109	The pool's parallelism comes from running N worker threads concurrently
110	on N cores. Each worker is sitting inside a single dispatch task at any
111	given moment. If a box function does something that takes a long time —
112	`sleep`, blocking I/O, a synchronous network request, waiting on a long-
113	running subprocess — **the worker thread is occupied for the full
114	duration**. It cannot pick up other tasks while it waits.
115	
116	Concretely:
117	- 16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10 seconds → the other 15 workers
118	  continue normally.
119	- 16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, no other
120	  task runs until a sleep finishes.
121	- The pool size is also the budget for "blocking activities". Heavy
122	  use of `sleep`-style boxes means raising `SORAMECH_WORKERS`.
123	
124	Why the runtime does not have a scheduler: SoraMech is deliberately not
125	in the business of "park this task and wake it at time T." There is no
126	delayed-spawn primitive, no timer thread, no polling loop. Adding one
127	would mean a second concurrency model alongside the pool, with its own
128	synchronization story. Instead, we lean on the pool's existing
129	mechanism: a task either runs (occupying a worker) or is blocked on a
130	slot waiting for a value (parked, no worker held). Long sleeps are an
131	"occupying a worker" case.
132	
133	For users who need many concurrent waits without burning workers, the
134	graph-level pattern is cooperative: split the operation into "kick off
135	the thing" (returns immediately) and "check whether the thing is done"
136	(returns immediately, returns a status), and wire them through an
137	iterator with a queued input. The iterator polls. No individual box
138	blocks for long. Each box completes quickly, freeing its worker.
139	
140	This is a documented constraint, not a bug. Box authors should know
141	that an unbounded `sleep` inside a function is the equivalent of
142	holding a worker hostage. The cooperative pattern is the way around
143	it.
144	
145	---
146	
147	## The three IPC options
148	
149	### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)
150	
151	The Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared
152	library (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.
153	You provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the
154	compiled library (`ffi.load("./mybox.so")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU
155	jumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.
156	
157	Since the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),
158	compiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).
159	The box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function
160	with typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.
161	
162	**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.
163	Bash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.
164	FFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.
165	
166	**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes
167	`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if
168	you handle the extension.
169	
170	---
171	
172	### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)
173	
174	`shm_open("/soramech-wire-0", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by
175	the kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it
176	into the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same
177	name gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is
178	immediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.
179	
180	For SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared
181	memory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write
182	calls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:
183	
184	- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc
185	- C: natively
186	- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is
187	  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`
188	
189	**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer
190	dereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this
191	is essentially free.
192	
193	**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header
194	(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and
195	a synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None
196	of these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but
197	the compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.
198	
199	**Cross-platform:**
200	- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.
201	- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No
202	  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.
203	- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).
204	  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.
205	
206	Shared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem
207	shortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.
208	
209	---
210	
211	### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)
212	
213	A Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an
214	IP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process
215	on the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel
216	routes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,
217	no protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.
218	
219	Unlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find
220	without inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;
221	each gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.
222	
223	**The model for SoraMech:**
224	
225	Each language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance
226	per language per worker thread:
227	
228	```
229	/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime
230	/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime
231	/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime
232	```
233	
234	The server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and
235	accepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker
236	connects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +
237	arguments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a
238	small script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the
239	function, and writes the result.
240	
241	**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian
242	integer (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The
243	receiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values
244	containing newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.
245	
246	**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero
247	CPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads
248	= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.
249	
250	**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**
251	
252	With LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language
253	call does this:
254	1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)
255	2. Send the request
256	3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler
257	4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`
258	5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine
259	6. Coroutine reads the response and continues
260	
261	The cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in
262	other coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.
263	
264	**Integration with the SoraMech thread pool (Stage 3):**
265	
266	Each worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls
267	a cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread
268	blocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on
269	other cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS
270	schedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned
271	to different workers can run simultaneously.
272	
273	**Cross-platform:**
274	- Linux: full support.
275	- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.
276	- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work
277	  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.
278	
279	Unix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also
280	supports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler
281	output and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.
282	
283	---
284	
285	## Summary comparison
286	
287	| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |
288	|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|
289	| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |
290	| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |
291	| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |
292	| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |
293	| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |
294	| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |
295	| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |
296	
297	*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.
298	
299	The compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is
300	compiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.
301	Same-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.
302	
303	---
304	
305	## Relevant files
306	
307	- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue
308	- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path
309	- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls
310	- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design
311	- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes
312	- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages
313	
```

1	# SoraMech — Writing a Language Spec
2	
3	## Status
4	Stub. Filled out as the phase 3 specs are implemented (issues
5	306–308). For the formal contract, see issue 303. For the existing
6	overview, see `docs/003-driver-system.md`.
7	
8	## What this doc will cover (when complete)
9	
10	A walk-through of writing a new language spec, intended for a user
11	adding Python, Rust, Haskell, or any language not shipped by default.
12	Sections to fill in once the reference specs are written:
13	
14	- **The contract.** What `lang_spec_t` requires you to provide
15	  (`init`, `teardown`, `compile`, `invoke`). Pointer to issue 303.
16	- **In-process vs out-of-process.** Lua and C run in the worker
17	  thread directly; Bash talks to a persistent subprocess over a
18	  socket. Which model fits your language depends on whether it has
19	  an embeddable runtime. Pointer to `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.
20	- **Walkthrough: the Lua spec.** The simplest reference. Covers
21	  per-worker `lua_State`, registry-based file caching, typed input
22	  marshalling, return-value serialization. Pointer to issue 306.
23	- **Walkthrough: the C spec.** Adds compile-time wrapper generation
24	  for arbitrary user functions. Pointer to issue 307.
25	- **Walkthrough: the Bash spec.** The out-of-process model. Wire
26	  protocol, framed length-prefix messages, persistent subprocess
27	  lifecycle. Pointer to issue 308.
28	- **Adding a new language.** Directory layout, Makefile, the bare
29	  minimum to link against the spec interface, dropping the result
30	  into `langs/<name>/`.
31	- **Thread safety.** Per-worker state isolation. The C spec's
32	  `static` and `globals` race story (issue 307); cooperative
33	  patterns for languages with mutable global state.
34	- **Error handling.** Hard-crash policy (issue 303). What
35	  language-level errors look like at the spec boundary. How to
36	  catch them without losing context.
37	
38	## Editor lexer (`langs/<name>/lexer.js`)
39	
40	Independent of the runtime spec, each language carries an editor
41	lexer that the source viewer (issue 215) uses to syntax-highlight
42	file content. The lexer ships in the same `langs/<name>/` directory
43	as the runtime spec — co-located by language, not by concern.
44	
45	### Contract
46	
47	A lexer is an ES module that exports a single function:
48	
49	```js
50	export function tokenize(text) {
51	  return [
52	    { type: 'keyword', start: 0,  end: 5 },
53	    { type: 'plain',   start: 5,  end: 6 },
54	    { type: 'string',  start: 6,  end: 17 },
55	    // ...
56	  ];
57	}
58	```
59	
60	The returned tokens must be ordered, gap-free, and cover the entire
61	input. Each token's `type` is a free-form string; the viewer applies
62	a CSS class `syntax-<type>`. The standard set is:
63	
64	| type        | typical use                                      |
65	|-------------|--------------------------------------------------|
66	| `keyword`   | language keywords                                |
67	| `comment`   | line and block comments                          |
68	| `string`    | quoted strings, char literals, here-docs         |
69	| `number`    | numeric literals                                 |
70	| `operator`  | `+`, `-`, `==`, `=`, `:`, …                      |
71	| `identifier`| variable / function names                        |
72	| `plain`     | whitespace and unclassified runs                 |
73	
74	Unknown types fall back to `syntax-default`. Lexers are free to
75	introduce custom types (`regex`, `annotation`, `decorator`); the
76	viewer just renders them with the default style unless someone adds
77	matching CSS.
78	
79	### Loading
80	
81	The viewer maps a file's extension to a language name (e.g.
82	`.lua` → `lua`, `.sh` → `bash`, `.c` / `.h` → `c`) and dynamically
83	imports `/langs/<name>/lexer.js` on first use. Result is cached for
84	the rest of the session. Files with an unknown extension or a
85	missing lexer fall back to plain rendering.
86	
87	### Reference implementations
88	
89	- `langs/lua/lexer.js` — hand-rolled state machine, ~150 lines.
90	  Covers `--` and `--[[ ]]` comments, single/double/long-bracket
91	  strings, hex / decimal / exponent numbers, identifiers,
92	  multi-char operators.
93	- `langs/bash/lexer.js` — same shape, with `$var` / `${...}` /
94	  `$(...)` expansions tagged as identifiers and `#` line comments
95	  detected only at line-start or after whitespace (not mid-token).
96	- `langs/c/lexer.js` — `//` line and `/* */` block comments,
97	  `#directive` lines tagged as keyword spans, hex and float
98	  literals with C suffix support.
99	
100	The reference lexers are starting points — extend or replace as
101	needed for languages with subtler syntax (regex literals, nested
102	template strings, indentation-sensitive parsing).
103	
104	## Why a stub now
105	
106	Issues 303, 306, 307, and 308 reference this document. Creating a
107	placeholder establishes the file path and the table of contents
108	above so cross-references resolve. The full content is written
109	incrementally as the reference specs are implemented and there is
110	real code to walk through.
111	
112	## Relevant issues
113	
114	- 303 — language runtime spec (the contract)
115	- 306 — Lua language spec
116	- 307 — C language spec
117	- 308 — Bash language spec
118	- `docs/003-driver-system.md` — phase 2 driver overview, phase 3
119	  spec overview
120	- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options and threading
121	  roadmap
122	
```

font-size:0.95rem; transform:rotate(-2deg)\">strings flow like ink ↗</span>\n        </div>\n      </div>`;\n\n    aside.innerHTML = `\n      ${brand}\n      <span class=\"toc-label\">Documents</span>\n      <ul class=\"toc-list\">${tocItems}</ul>\n      ${foot}\n    `;\n\n    // Sub-nav from page <h2> elements\n    const subnav = aside.querySelector(\"[data-subnav]\");\n    if (subnav) {\n      const heads = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll(\"main h2[id]\"));\n      subnav.innerHTML = heads.map(h =>\n        `<li><a href=\"#${h.id}\" data-sub-target=\"${h.id}\">${h.textContent.trim()}</a></li>`\n      ).join(\"\");\n\n      // Scroll spy\n      const linkFor = id => subnav.querySelector(`[data-sub-target=\"${CSS.escape(id)}\"]`);\n      const obs = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {\n        entries.forEach(e => {\n          const a = linkFor(e.target.id);\n          if (!a) return;\n          if (e.isIntersecting) {\n            subnav.querySelectorAll(\"a\").forEach(x => x.classList.remove(\"current\"));\n            a.classList.add(\"current\");\n          }\n        });\n      }, { rootMargin: \"-20% 0px -70% 0px\" });\n      heads.forEach(h => obs.observe(h));\n    }\n\n    // Number every page-level h2 in the document using its data-num if present,\n    // otherwise inject section numbers like \"§01.A\" sequentially.\n    const h2s = document.querySelectorAll(\"main h2\");\n    let n = 0;\n    h2s.forEach(h => {\n      if (h.hasAttribute(\"data-num\")) return;\n      n++;\n      const letter = String.fromCharCode(64 + n); // A, B, C\n      const ts = (document.body.dataset.page || \"\").match(/(\\d{3})/);\n      const docNum = ts ? ts[1].slice(1) : \"00\";\n      h.setAttribute(\"data-num\", `§${docNum}.${letter}`);\n    });\n  }\n\n  document.addEventListener(\"DOMContentLoaded\", build);\n})();\n",
  "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/HTML/assets/nav.js"
}

The runner is invoked separately, by command line. <code>last-run.jsonl</code> is the runner's output, consumed by external tooling, not by the editor.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"runner-2\">Phase 2 runner — src/007-runner-main.lua</h3>\n        <p>Synchronous Lua interpreter. It is <em>not</em> where file-source boxes read from — those read arbitrary paths via the <code>data</code> box kind.\n        </div>\n\n        <h2 id=\"box\">Box file format</h2>\n        <p>Every box is a single JSON file under <code>boxes/&lt;id&gt;.json</code>. Every box has exactly <strong>one output wire</strong> (issue 218). There is no <code>outputs</code> array. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output wire as one value; multi-value returns are encoded as JSON (or a language-native struct on a same-language wire) and decoded downstream.</p>\n\n        <h3 id=\"box-kinds\">Box kinds</h3>\n        <table>\n          <thead><tr><th>kind</th><th>Runs a function?</th><th>Notes</th></tr></thead>\n          <tbody>\n            <tr><td><code>call</code></td><td>yes</td><td>Plain call, comparator, iterator, etc. — see <code>routing</code> below.</td></tr>\n            <tr><td><code>data</code></td><td>no</td><td>Language-agnostic <strong>file source</strong>. Writes inputs to disk.</td></tr>\n          </tbody>\n        </table>\n        <p><code>data</code> and <code>file_write</code> are dispatch-layer primitives — the runtime reads/writes the file directly, no language spec is invoked. Both follow atomic-write semantics where it matters (write to <code>path.tmp</code>, fsync, rename).</p>\n<pre data-lang=\"json\">{ \"id\": \"config\", \"kind\": \"data\", \"path\": \"config.json\",\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"save\",   \"kind\": \"file_write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"path\", \"type\": \"string\" },\n    { \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 400, \"y\": 100 } }</pre>\n\n        <h3 id=\"routing\">Call boxes and the <code>routing</code> field</h3>\n        <p>A <code>call</code> box runs a function (<code>ref</code> + <code>fn</code>) and produces one output value. Routing decides which downstream branch receives the function's output; the function itself doesn't know.</p>\n\n        <h4>Routing kinds</h4>\n        <table>\n          <thead><tr><th>routing.kind</th><th>Output ports</th><th>Branch picker</th><th>Status</th></tr></thead>\n          <tbody>\n            <tr><td><code>plain</code></td>       <td>single port</td>
